topic: Day 2 · Hypernatraemia & the Perils of Correction
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Intensive Care Unit
speakerBio: Intensivist-nephrologist whose signature teaching line is 'the drip is a drug — prescribe the rate, not just the bag', and who has spent a career keeping sodium moving at a brain-safe pace.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Two patients, two disasters waiting to happen, one lesson. In bed 4, an 88-year-old man from a care home with advanced dementia is admitted with a chest infection: Na⁺ 168 mmol/L, hypotensive, cracked lips, urine like syrup. In bed 6, a malnourished alcoholic woman found collapsed has Na⁺ 104, and the night registrar has already run in a litre of 3% saline. Both patients can be killed not by their electrolyte, but by how fast we move it. This is the session about the intravenous drip as a weapon: how to correct sodium in both directions without infarcting or dissolving the brain. Get the rate wrong and you turn a survivable metabolic derangement into a permanent neurological catastrophe.

1 · 💧 Hypernatraemia is ALWAYS a water deficit

Mirror image of session 9. Where hyponatraemia is water excess, hypernatraemia is always a deficit of water relative to sodium. You cannot become hypernatraemic if you have a working thirst mechanism and access to water — you would simply drink. So hypernatraemia is, at its core, a disease of people who cannot drink: the very old, the very young, the intubated, the neurologically impaired, the bedbound.

Hypernatraemia = not enough water. Ask two questions: "why can't this patient drink to their thirst?" and "where is the water going?"

Defence against a rising sodium is two-limbed: thirst (drives water intake) and ADH (concentrates urine to retain water). Sustained hypernatraemia means at least one limb has failed — usually thirst/access, sometimes ADH (diabetes insipidus).

MechanismExamplesUrine osmolality
Pure water lossFever/insensible loss, diabetes insipidus, respiratory lossesDI: inappropriately dilute; insensible: concentrated
Hypotonic fluid loss (water > sodium)Osmotic diuresis (hyperglycaemia, mannitol, high-protein feed), diarrhoea (esp. children), loop diuretics, post-obstructive/ATN diuresisVariable, often ~300–600
Sodium gain (rare)Hypertonic saline/bicarbonate infusion, salt poisoning, hyperaldosteronismConcentrated, high urine Na
Impaired thirst/accessDementia, stroke, sedation, restraint, infants, adipsic hypernatraemiaAppropriately concentrated (>700)
💡 The bedside triage

Look at the urine. A hypernatraemic patient with concentrated urine (>700 mOsm/kg) has an intact kidney conserving water — the problem is intake/insensible loss. A hypernatraemic patient still passing dilute urine (<300) despite a high plasma sodium has a kidney that can't concentrate — that is diabetes insipidus until proven otherwise.

2 · 🚰 Diabetes insipidus — central vs nephrogenic

DI is failure of the ADH axis: either the pituitary doesn't make ADH (central/cranial) or the kidney doesn't respond to it (nephrogenic). Both produce large volumes of inappropriately dilute urine (polyuria >3 L/day) and, if water access is limited, hypernatraemia.

FeatureCentral (cranial) DINephrogenic DI
Defect↓ ADH production/release (posterior pituitary)Kidney resistant to ADH
CausesPituitary surgery/tumour, trauma, infiltration (sarcoid, histiocytosis), hypoxic injury, idiopathic/autoimmuneLithium, chronic hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, chronic renal disease, congenital (AVPR2/AQP2)
Response to desmopressin (DDAVP)Urine concentrates >50% — it worksLittle/no response — kidney can't hear it
TreatmentDesmopressin (DDAVP) replacementRemove cause; thiazide + low-salt diet, amiloride (for lithium), NSAID; correct Ca/K

The water-deprivation test

The classic discriminator when the diagnosis is unclear (and the patient is not already hypernatraemic):

  1. Deprive of water under supervision, measuring hourly urine and plasma osmolality and weight. Normal kidney concentrates urine (>700) and plasma osmolality stays normal.
  2. Primary polydipsia: urine concentrates appropriately on deprivation (the axis is intact — they were just over-drinking).
  3. DI: urine stays dilute despite rising plasma osmolality. Now give desmopressin.
  4. Central DI: urine osmolality jumps >50% after DDAVP. Nephrogenic DI: minimal response.
⚠️ Stop the deprivation test if the patient loses >3% body weight or becomes hypernatraemic/hypotensive

The test deliberately dehydrates the patient — in true DI they can lose litres fast. Weigh them, cap weight loss at 3%, and never start the test in someone who is already hypernatraemic. Newer assays for copeptin (a stable surrogate for ADH) are increasingly replacing the traditional deprivation test for safety and accuracy.

3 · 🧮 The free-water deficit — how much water is missing

Before you can correct hypernatraemia you must estimate the deficit. The standard formula:

Free-water deficit (L) = Total body water × [(current Na⁺ / target Na⁺) − 1]
where Total body water ≈ 0.6 × weight (kg) in men, 0.5 × in women (0.45–0.5 in the elderly).

Worked example (our bed-4 patient): 70 kg man, Na⁺ 168, target 140. TBW = 0.6 × 70 = 42 L. Deficit = 42 × (168/140 − 1) = 42 × 0.20 = 8.4 L. That is the pure-water deficit; you must also add ongoing losses (insensible ~1 L/day, urine output) and, if the patient is shocked, restore circulating volume with isotonic fluid FIRST.

💡 Resuscitate the circulation before you chase the sodium

A hypovolaemic, hypotensive hypernatraemic patient (like our care-home man) needs 0.9% saline to restore perfusion first — even though it is "salty," it is hypotonic relative to his plasma of 168 and it fixes the shock. Once he is haemodynamically stable, switch to hypotonic fluid (5% dextrose, 0.45% saline, or enteral water) to replace the free-water deficit slowly.

4 · 🐢 Safe correction of hypernatraemia — slow, or the brain swells

Here is the symmetry with hyponatraemia. In chronic hypernatraemia the brain adapts by generating intracellular "idiogenic osmoles" to stop itself shrivelling. If you now drop the plasma sodium fast, water rushes down the osmotic gradient into those solute-loaded brain cells → cerebral oedema, seizures, herniation, death.

Lower the sodium no faster than ~10 mmol/L per 24 hours in chronic hypernatraemia (≈0.5 mmol/L/hour). Aim for full correction over 48–72h, not overnight.
  • Acute hypernatraemia (<48h, e.g. iatrogenic salt load) — the brain has not adapted, so it can be corrected faster and more safely (~1 mmol/L/h).
  • Chronic / unknown duration — assume adapted; cap at 10 mmol/L/24h.
  • Recheck sodium every 4–6 hours and recalculate; use the enteral route (water via NG) whenever possible — it is the safest, most physiological correction.
⚠️ The paediatric and post-DKA cerebral-oedema trap

Children with hypernatraemic dehydration and patients being resuscitated from HHS/DKA are exquisitely vulnerable to cerebral oedema from over-rapid sodium lowering. Slow, measured rehydration with frequent sodium checks — not aggressive free-water boluses — is the rule. A falling sodium that outpaces 10 mmol/L/24h should trigger you to slow the infusion, not celebrate.

5 · ⏳ The other direction — osmotic demyelination from correcting hyponatraemia too FAST

Now the headline danger, the one that follows straight from session 9. When hyponatraemia is chronic (>48h), the brain has extruded organic osmolytes to stop swelling. Correct the sodium too quickly and the brain cells, now osmolyte-depleted, shrink violently and demyelinate. This is osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), historically called central pontine myelinolysis (though extrapontine sites — basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum — are also hit).

The clinical course — a cruel biphasic story

  • The patient initially improves as the sodium rises and the acute encephalopathy lifts. Everyone relaxes.
  • Then, 2–6 days later, a new, devastating neurology emerges: dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, and in the worst cases the "locked-in" syndrome — awake, aware, unable to move or speak.
  • MRI changes lag by 1–2 weeks (symmetrical pontine signal change); a normal early MRI does not exclude it. Outcome ranges from partial recovery to permanent disability or death; there is no specific treatment — prevention is everything.
🎯 Why ODS is a disease of over-treatment, not of low sodium itself

The pons doesn't demyelinate because the sodium was low; it demyelinates because the sodium rose too fast before the brain could re-import protective osmolytes (which takes days). That is why a rushed correction is far more dangerous than the hyponatraemia it was treating. The whole discipline of section 6 is about not letting the sodium run away from you.

6 · ⛔ The correction ceiling for hyponatraemia — and the high-risk patient

The European (ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA 2014) limits, now standard of care:

PatientMax rise in first 24 hMax rise in 48 h
Standard risk≤ 10 mmol/L≤ 18 mmol/L
High risk (aim lower)≤ 8 mmol/L (many aim 4–6)≤ 16 mmol/L

Who is the high-risk patient? The features that make the brain fragile and correction likely to overshoot:

  • Serum sodium ≤ 105 mmol/L — the deeper the hyponatraemia, the more osmolyte-depleted the brain.
  • Chronic alcohol use / alcoholism.
  • Malnutrition (including anorexia, cachexia).
  • Hypokalaemia — replacing potassium also raises the effective osmolality and drives sodium up; count K⁺ replacement into your correction.
  • Advanced liver disease (e.g. awaiting transplant).
⚠️ The autocorrection ambush — when ADH switches off

The single commonest way to overcorrect is not the fluid you prescribe — it is the kidney taking over. In hypovolaemic or thiazide-induced hyponatraemia, once you restore volume (or stop the drug), the ADH stimulus vanishes and the kidney dumps litres of dilute urine, and the sodium rockets on its own. A sudden brisk diuresis in a patient you are correcting is a RED ALERT: recheck the sodium urgently, because you may already be overshooting.

7 · 🔄 Re-lowering an overcorrected sodium — the rescue

If you have exceeded (or are about to exceed) the ceiling, you can and should re-lower the sodium to pull it back under the 24-hour limit. This is a recognised, guideline-endorsed rescue:

  1. 5% dextrose (electrolyte-free water) IV — e.g. 3 mL/kg/h — to add free water and bring the sodium back down.
  2. Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2–4 micrograms IV/SC — switch ADH back "on" to stop the runaway free-water diuresis and lock the sodium in place.
  3. A proactive strategy in high-risk deep hyponatraemia is the "DDAVP clamp": give scheduled desmopressin from the outset and raise the sodium in a slow, controlled way with hypertonic saline, so the kidney can never surprise you with an autocorrection.
Overshot the sodium? Give free water (5% dextrose) and desmopressin to bring it back down. Re-lowering is not defeat — it prevents osmotic demyelination.
💡 Target the numbers, monitor obsessively

During active correction of severe hyponatraemia, check the sodium every 2 hours. Set the day's ceiling in your head before you start (say +8 from a baseline of 106 → do not exceed 114 by this time tomorrow). If you hit it early, STOP raising and hold; if you blow past it, re-lower. Frequent measurement is the whole game.

8 · 🧭 Master table — the two directions, side by side

Over-rapid correction of HYPOnatraemiaOver-rapid correction of HYPERnatraemia
InjuryOsmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS / central pontine myelinolysis)Cerebral oedema
Direction of Na changeSodium raised too fast → brain shrinks/demyelinatesSodium lowered too fast → brain swells
Safe rate≤10 mmol/L/24h (≤8, aim 4–6 if high-risk)≤10 mmol/L/24h (chronic)
Timing of harmBiphasic — deteriorates 2–6 days laterHours — during correction
RescueRe-lower with 5% dextrose + desmopressinSlow the infusion; hypertonic saline if seizing from oedema
PreventionCap the rise, 2-hourly Na, DDAVP clamp in high-riskCap the fall, 4–6 hourly Na, enteral water
🎯 The unifying rule of the drip

Whatever direction you are moving the sodium, the brain has adapted to whatever it has lived with for >48 hours, and it can only re-adapt slowly. ~10 mmol/L per 24 hours is the universal speed limit in either direction for chronic derangement — tighter (~8) for high-risk hyponatraemia. Move the number gently and the brain follows; move it fast and the brain breaks.

☠️ M&M — the alcoholic woman who was corrected in a day

A 46-year-old woman with alcohol dependence and severe malnutrition was found collapsed: Na⁺ 104, K⁺ 2.6, chronic (weeks of poor intake, vomiting, thiazide for hypertension). She was drowsy but not seizing. The night team, alarmed by the number, gave repeated 3% saline and 2 L of 0.9% saline, and replaced her potassium aggressively. By the next morning her sodium was 126 — a rise of 22 mmol/L in under 24 hours. Three separate mechanisms had stacked: the hypertonic saline, the volume repletion switching off ADH (a massive autocorrective diuresis followed stopping the thiazide), and the potassium replacement each pushing the sodium up. She woke, seemed better, then on day 4 became mute and quadriparetic — locked-in from osmotic demyelination. Every one of her risk factors was textbook: Na ≤105, alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia. Lessons: (1) in the high-risk patient aim for only 4–6 mmol/L/24h; (2) count potassium replacement as part of the sodium correction; (3) watch for the autocorrective diuresis when ADH switches off and pre-empt it with a DDAVP clamp; (4) the moment she crossed the ceiling, the team should have re-lowered her with 5% dextrose and desmopressin. The hyponatraemia was survivable; the correction was not.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Hypernatraemia is always a water deficit — usually a patient who cannot drink; check the urine to separate DI (dilute) from intake/insensible loss (concentrated).
  2. Central vs nephrogenic DI = the desmopressin response — central concentrates >50%, nephrogenic doesn't; think lithium and hypercalcaemia for nephrogenic.
  3. Calculate the free-water deficit (TBW × [Na/target − 1]), resuscitate shock with saline first, then replace water slowly.
  4. Correct hypernatraemia at ≤10 mmol/L/24h — faster causes cerebral oedema, especially in children and post-DKA/HHS.
  5. Correct hyponatraemia at ≤10 mmol/L/24h (≤8, aim 4–6 in high-risk) — faster causes osmotic demyelination (biphasic, devastating, untreatable).
  6. The high-risk patient: Na ≤105, alcohol, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease — and beware the autocorrective diuresis when ADH switches off.
  7. Overshot? Re-lower with 5% dextrose + desmopressin. Check the sodium every 2 hours during correction — measurement is prevention.

moderatorQs.q: A hypernatraemic patient (Na 165) is passing large volumes of dilute urine. How do you distinguish central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and how does that change management?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Dilute urine in the face of a high plasma sodium means the kidney can't concentrate — diabetes insipidus. The discriminator is the response to desmopressin (DDAVP): in central (cranial) DI the pituitary isn't making ADH, so exogenous DDAVP works and the urine osmolality rises by more than 50%; in nephrogenic DI the kidney is resistant, so there is little or no response. This changes everything: central DI is treated by replacing the hormone (desmopressin), whereas nephrogenic DI is treated by removing the cause (classically lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia) and using a thiazide, low-salt diet, amiloride (for lithium) or NSAID. A copeptin assay is increasingly used to make this call more safely than a formal water-deprivation test.

moderatorQs.q: Explain why correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly causes osmotic demyelination but the hyponatraemia itself did not.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: In chronic hyponatraemia the brain protects itself from swelling by extruding organic osmolytes over 24–48 hours, so it sits at a new, lower intracellular osmolality in equilibrium with the low plasma sodium. That is why chronic hyponatraemia is often surprisingly well-tolerated. If you then raise the plasma sodium faster than the brain can re-import those osmolytes (which takes days), the brain cells are suddenly hypotonic relative to plasma, water is drawn out, they shrink and the myelin sheaths break down — osmotic demyelination syndrome, classically central pontine myelinolysis. So the damage is caused by the speed of correction, not the low sodium itself — which is exactly why the ceiling of ≤10 (≤8 in high-risk) mmol/L per 24h exists.

moderatorQs.q: You are correcting a patient with Na 106 and suddenly they start passing 400 mL/h of dilute urine. What is happening and what do you do?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is the autocorrective (aquaretic) diuresis — the single commonest cause of inadvertent overcorrection. The patient's hyponatraemia was ADH-driven (hypovolaemia or a thiazide); once you restored volume or stopped the drug, the ADH stimulus vanished, the kidney switched to dumping electrolyte-free water, and the sodium is now rising rapidly on its own — on top of any fluid you are giving. This is a red alert for impending osmotic demyelination. I would recheck the sodium immediately and then 2-hourly, stop any hypertonic saline, and if the projected rise exceeds the day's ceiling, actively re-lower with 5% dextrose and desmopressin 2–4 micrograms to switch ADH back on and clamp the sodium. In a high-risk patient I'd ideally have pre-empted this with a scheduled DDAVP clamp from the start.

audienceQs.q: My hypernatraemic patient at Na 170 is also hypotensive. Do I give free water or saline first?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Saline first — resuscitate the circulation before you chase the sodium. A shocked patient needs restored perfusion now, and 0.9% saline, although 'salty', is actually hypotonic relative to a plasma of 170, so it both fixes the haemodynamics and begins gently lowering the sodium. Once the patient is haemodynamically stable, switch to hypotonic fluid (5% dextrose, 0.45% saline, or enteral water via NG — the safest route) to replace the calculated free-water deficit (TBW × [Na/target − 1]) plus ongoing losses. Then hold the fall to ≤10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid cerebral oedema, rechecking the sodium every 4–6 hours.

audienceQs.q: When I replace potassium in a hyponatraemic patient, does that affect the sodium correction?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes, and it catches people out. Potassium is osmotically active, so infused potassium raises the effective plasma osmolality and pushes the sodium up too — it counts towards your 24-hour sodium correction, on top of whatever saline you give. In a high-risk patient (often the malnourished, alcoholic, hypokalaemic one) aggressive potassium replacement can be the hidden reason the sodium overshoots into the osmotic-demyelination zone. So: include the potassium you plan to give in your correction estimate, keep the total sodium rise to ≤8 mmol/L/24h in high-risk patients, and monitor the sodium every 2 hours during active correction.

audienceQs.q: A patient corrected too fast three days ago is now developing dysarthria and weakness. Is it too late to do anything?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Once osmotic demyelination is established there is no specific proven treatment — management is supportive (airway/swallow protection, rehabilitation), and the MRI changes may lag the clinical picture by one to two weeks, so a normal early scan doesn't exclude it. The key window is before symptoms appear: if a patient has been overcorrected but not yet developed ODS, re-lowering the sodium with 5% dextrose and desmopressin has been reported to prevent or attenuate demyelination, so it is still worth acting on a documented overshoot even after the fact. Outcomes are variable — some patients make a surprising partial recovery over months — so aggressive supportive care and rehab are warranted rather than nihilism.
